The Split

The Story of Islam

The Split

Sunni, Shia, and Karbala

In plain English — the day one community walked two roads, and the field that bound them together for ever

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it out loud. This story is made to be told. Read slowly, as if you were sitting with everyone at home — with the morning of Damascus, the letters from Kufa, and the silence of the field of Karbala.

The story is told straight — the meaning of tradition's words is given in this book's own plain English, not as word-for-word quotations. Where a saying is given directly, the book says plainly that it is tradition's account.

The green box at the end of each part — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask the question. Let the listener speak. In this story these questions matter as much as the story — because this story ends on a question that has never been answered.

There are two kinds of things in this book — verses of the Quran and the evidence of history, like old manuscripts and the books of scholars; and the stories of tradition, told for centuries in the books of the Seerah and the Hadith. Where the story is tradition's, the book says so plainly — 'tradition says'. Where something rests on evidence, the book names it.

There is no picture of the Prophet Muhammad in this book — not as a man, not as a child, not as an infant, not in shadow, not from behind. And there is no recognisable picture of Husayn, Ali, or any member of the Prophet's family either. The pictures in this book show only the desert, the river, the tents, the lamps, the mosque and geometric ornament — no person at all.

The main story of this book comes from the Quran, the books of Hadith, al-Tabari's History, al-Baladhuri's Ansab, and modern scholars. The full list of sources is at the end of the book.

In this book both the Sunni and the Shia accounts are recorded in their own notes, fully and honestly. This book takes no one's side — and it does not decide who was right. That question is recorded separately in Part 8 of this book — left open, to this day.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Muawiya ibn Abi Sufyan (d. 680) — the long-time governor of Syria (Sham); Ali's opponent; Caliph after Siffin (661–680). The first Caliph of the Umayyad house.

Hasan ibn Ali (d. 670) — the elder son of Ali and Fatima, the Prophet's grandson; Caliph for a few months after Ali, then made peace with Muawiya and returned to Medina.

Husayn ibn Ali (d. 680) — the younger son of Ali and Fatima, the Prophet's grandson; killed at Karbala.

Yazid ibn Muawiya (d. 683) — Muawiya's son; became Caliph in 680 — tradition says he was the first Caliph whom his father had named as successor in his own lifetime.

Zaynab bint Ali — the daughter of Ali and Fatima, Husayn's sister; taken captive to Damascus after Karbala, where tradition says she spoke fearlessly in the court.

Ali Zayn al-Abidin (d. about 713) — Husayn's son; the only man of the family to survive Karbala — tradition says he was ill, and so did not go out to fight. The fourth Imam in Shia tradition.

Mukhtar ibn Abi Ubayd (d. 687) — a chief of Kufa; rose up a few years after Karbala and said he would avenge Husayn's killers.

The people of Kufa — the people of the city of Kufa in Iraq; tradition says they wrote hundreds of letters inviting Husayn, and then did not stand by him when he came.

1 · After Ali — Muawiya and the Umayyad Turn · · AFTER ALI — MUAWIYA AND THE UMAYYAD TURN, 661–680

661. Ali had been assassinated — and the community stood again before the same question that had arisen on the day the Prophet died — who now? Ali's son Hasan was recognised as Caliph in Kufa — but in Syria stood Muawiya, who had the greatest army, and who had claimed the caliphate ever since Siffin.

Muawiya was no new man. He had been governor of Syria for twenty years — tradition says Umar had placed him there, and Uthman had kept him there. Syria was his own place — its people knew him, and its army was his. And Muawiya made Damascus his capital — far from Medina, an old Roman city, from which the community would now be ruled.

With Muawiya came a great change — the caliphate was no longer Medina's, it was Damascus's. The first Caliphs had lived in Medina — near the mosque, among the people, in simplicity. Now the Caliph would live in a city — with a court, with officials, and like a kingdom. Tradition says Muawiya said — 'I am the first king.' That saying is tradition's, but its meaning was plain — the caliphate had begun to look like a kingship.

Muawiya built a kingdom — tradition says he set up the postal service, made the army firm, and built ships at sea — there was even an attack on Constantinople in his time, but the city could not be taken. He also made the bayt al-mal (the treasury) firm — now the sharing of money was decided from Damascus.

Muawiya's twenty years — 661 to 680 — begin in tradition with the 'Am al-Jama'a' (the Year of Unity) — the year when the community came under one roof again. But that unity was a peace — and Hasan had paid the price of the peace. Its story is in the next part.

Muawiya's twenty years — tradition's dates

The time of Muawiya's caliphate, 661–680 — is tradition's date, from al-Tabari's History and al-Baladhuri's Ansab. Making Damascus the capital, and setting up the postal service and the army, also come from tradition.

'I am the first king' — a story of tradition

Muawiya's saying — 'I am the first king' — is a story of tradition, recorded in al-Tabari's History. Modern scholars, like Fred Donner, say that in Muawiya's time the caliphate truly began to become like a kingdom — with a court, officials, and the capital at Damascus.

Pause and think — Muawiya moved the caliphate from Medina to Damascus and made it a kingdom. Should the rule of a faith have become a kingdom — or should it have stayed in the simplicity of Medina?

2 · The Peace of Hasan — The Treaty That Stopped the War · · THE PEACE OF HASAN — THE TREATY THAT STOPPED THE WAR, 661

After Ali's assassination, Hasan became Caliph in Kufa — but only for a few months. Tradition says Hasan saw — his army was divided, the people of Kufa were tired, and Muawiya's army was large and united. Another war would have meant — more Muslim blood.

So Hasan made peace with Muawiya. Tradition says the terms of the treaty were these — Hasan would give up the caliphate; Muawiya would become Caliph; Hasan would be allowed to live in peace in Medina and would receive a pension from the treasury; and Ali's companions would be forgiven. The greatest term — tradition says — was this: Muawiya would name no successor after himself — the next Caliph would be chosen by a council.

Hasan gave up the caliphate and returned to Medina. Tradition says some people taunted him — 'You have abandoned us!' — and Hasan answered — 'I saved the blood of the community.' That year was called in tradition the 'Am al-Jama'a' — the Year of Unity.

Hasan died in Medina in 670 — by tradition's count, at only forty-five years of age. Of his death, tradition says he was given poison — and Shia tradition says this was done at Muawiya's order. That is tradition's account — and it is recorded in a separate note in this book, because scholars differ over its evidence.

The terms of the peace — stories of tradition, and differences in the sources

The terms of Hasan and Muawiya's peace — the pension, the forgiveness, and 'Muawiya will name no successor after himself' — come from al-Tabari's History and al-Baladhuri's Ansab. But the sources differ over which terms were really agreed — some accounts give a different sum for the pension, some give a different count of the terms. This book does not decide which account is right — the difference is between the sources themselves.

Hasan's death — the poison is tradition's account

The story that Hasan was given poison is a story of tradition — recorded in al-Tabari's History and al-Baladhuri's Ansab. That it was done at Muawiya's order is Shia tradition's account. Modern scholars, like Wilferd Madelung, record the story — but its evidence is disputed, and this book does not decide how Hasan died.

Pause and think — Hasan gave up the caliphate and stopped a war — and people taunted him for it. Can giving up ever be greater than winning — when giving up saves people's lives?

3 · Yazid — The Succession and the Demand for Allegiance · · YAZID — THE SUCCESSION AND THE DEMAND FOR ALLEGIANCE, 680

The greatest term of Hasan's peace — 'Muawiya will name no successor after himself' — tradition says Muawiya broke it. Before he died in 680, Muawiya named his son Yazid as his successor — and took people's allegiance to him.

This was the first time — tradition says — that a Caliph had named his own son as successor in his lifetime. Abu Bakr had named Umar — but Umar was not his son. Umar had made a council. Uthman and Ali too had been chosen by a council. Now the caliphate was beginning to pass from father to son — as it happens in a kingship.

After Muawiya's death, Yazid became Caliph — and he sent an order to the governor of Medina — take Husayn ibn Ali's allegiance — and if he refuses, arrest him. Yazid knew — until Husayn pledged allegiance, not everyone would accept his caliphate. Husayn was the Prophet's grandson — his very name was a challenge.

Tradition says Husayn said to the governor of Medina — 'Allegiance is not a thing given in hiding — it is given before everyone. Let me stay in Medina, and we will speak in the morning.' And that same night, tradition says, Husayn left Medina with his family and went to Mecca.

There were others in Medina who did not pledge allegiance either — tradition says Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr also went to Mecca. But Husayn's case was different — he was of the Prophet's house, and his allegiance would have meant — the Prophet's house putting its seal on Yazid's caliphate.

Yazid's naming — tradition's date

Muawiya's naming of Yazid as successor, and Yazid's becoming Caliph in 680 — is tradition's date, from al-Tabari's History. That it was the first time a father named his son — that is tradition's account.

The demand for allegiance — a story of tradition

Yazid's order to the governor of Medina — take Husayn's allegiance — comes from al-Tabari's History — a story of tradition. Husayn's words in reply are given a little differently in different accounts — this book gives their meaning, not a word-for-word quotation.

Pause and think — Muawiya gave the caliphate from father to son — and for the first time the caliphate looked like a kingship. Should a government become the property of one family — or should it be ruled by the people's choice?

4 · Husayn's Journey — From Mecca to Kufa · · HUSAYN'S JOURNEY — FROM MECCA TO KUFA, 680

In Mecca, letters from Kufa began to reach Husayn — tradition says hundreds of letters came — the people of Kufa were writing — 'Come, we have no ruler — come, we will pledge allegiance to you.' Kufa was Ali's city — its people loved Ali's house, and were angry with Yazid.

Husayn first sent his cousin Muslim ibn Aqil to Kufa — to see whether the people of Kufa were truly ready. Tradition says Muslim wrote — 'Kufa is ready — come.' But when Yazid's new governor Ubaydullah ibn Ziyad reached Kufa, the people grew afraid — and Muslim was left alone. Tradition says Muslim was killed in Kufa — before Husayn arrived there.

Husayn had not received this news. He had already left Mecca — on 8 Dhu al-Hijja, 60 AH — by tradition's count, in the very days of the Hajj. With him was his family — his wives, his children, his brothers, and his companions. Tradition says some people in Mecca stopped him — they said, do not go to Kufa, its people cannot be trusted. Tradition says Husayn answered — 'I have read Muslim's letter — and I am going.'

On the road, near Kufa, Husayn met the army of al-Hurr ibn Yazid — a thousand horsemen, by tradition's count. Al-Hurr said — 'I have orders not to let you go to Kufa — but I will not take you to Yazid either.' And Husayn's caravan stopped in the desert — in the field of Karbala, near the river Euphrates.

More troops came from Kufa — tradition says now before him stood the army of Umar ibn Sa'd — thousands of soldiers. And with Husayn — tradition says — there were seventy-two companions — his family and his friends. The water of the river was also cut off — tradition says the caravan was not allowed to take water from the Euphrates.

The letters from Kufa — tradition's dates and counts

The hundreds of letters from Kufa, Muslim ibn Aqil's going to Kufa and being killed there, and Husayn's leaving Mecca — come from al-Tabari's History — a story of tradition. The count of the letters is given differently in different accounts — some say a hundred, some say hundreds — this book says 'hundreds', with no fixed count.

Seventy-two companions — tradition's count

The count of seventy-two (72) companions with Husayn is tradition's count — from the maqtal accounts in al-Tabari's History. Other accounts give a slightly different count — some more than a hundred. This book calls 72 tradition's count, not a settled fact.

Pause and think — The people of Kufa invited Husayn — and then did not stand by him. Is inviting someone and then leaving them alone — a greater betrayal than never inviting them at all?

5 · Karbala (680) — The Tenth of Muharram · · KARBALA, 680 — THE TENTH OF MUHARRAM

◆ ◆ This part is not for younger listeners — it tells of a battle and of people dying, in a line or two, without any detail.

Tradition says that on 10 Muharram, 61 AH (10 October, 680), in the field of Karbala, there was a battle — of Husayn and his seventy-two companions, against an army of thousands.

Tradition says that on that day Husayn and his companions were killed — and the family of Husayn — the women and the children — were taken captive.

The story of Karbala — Tabari's maqtal accounts

The story of Karbala — the date of 10 Muharram, the battle, and Husayn's death — comes from the maqtal (martyrdom) material in al-Tabari's History, built on the accounts of Abu Mikhnaf. The story is tradition's — there is no contemporary document of it, and the details of the battle are given differently in different accounts. This book gives no detail of the battle — only that it happened, and that Husayn was killed.

The date — tradition's date

The date of Karbala, 10 Muharram, 61 AH — is tradition's date. In the common era it falls around 10 October, 680 — by tradition's count.

6 · The Aftermath — The Captives, Zaynab, and the Return to Medina · · THE AFTERMATH — THE CAPTIVES, ZAYNAB, AND THE RETURN TO MEDINA

◆ ◆ This part is not for younger listeners — it tells of captivity and of death, in a line or two, without any detail.

After Karbala, the family of Husayn — the women and the children — were taken first to Kufa, then to Damascus — to Yazid's court. With them was Ali Zayn al-Abidin — Husayn's son, who was ill.

Tradition says that in the court of Damascus Zaynab — Husayn's sister — stood up and spoke fearlessly — she told Yazid that what had happened was a wrong, and that God would not forget it. Her words are given a little differently in different accounts — this book gives their meaning, not a word-for-word quotation.

Tradition says that after some time Yazid released the captives — and they returned to Medina. A mourning fell over Medina — tradition says that when the caravan reached Medina, the whole city wept.

Yazid did not remain Caliph for long — tradition says he died in 683. After him his son Muawiya II was Caliph for a few months, then he gave up the caliphate — and a civil war broke out in the community again — the Second Fitna.

Zaynab's speech — a story of tradition

The story of Zaynab's speech in the court is a story of tradition — it is not in al-Tabari's History, but is recorded in later Shia books of tradition. Her words have many forms — this book gives their meaning, not a fixed quotation.

The Second Fitna — tradition's dates

Yazid's death in 683 and Muawiya II's being Caliph for a few months — are tradition's dates, from al-Tabari's History.

7 · The Mourning — Ashura, the Majlis, and Remembrance Across the Centuries · · THE MOURNING — ASHURA, THE MAJLIS, AND REMEMBRANCE ACROSS THE CENTURIES

Ever since Karbala, every year on the tenth of Muharram — Ashura — Husayn is remembered. This remembrance is not of one day only — for the first ten days of Muharram, and then until the fortieth day, Arbaeen, people gather — they sit in the majlis, they hear the story of Karbala, and they recite marsiya (poetry of mourning).

In the majlis the storyteller — the zakir — tells the story of Karbala, and the listeners weep. In some places people take out a procession — they walk the streets, and they carry the alam (the standard) — in memory of the tents of Karbala. In Iraq, millions of people go on pilgrimage to Karbala — and on Arbaeen, tens of millions walk on foot — tradition says it is one of the largest walking pilgrimages in the world.

The ways of mourning are not the same everywhere. Some people mourn by beating their chests with their hands — sina-zani. Some mourn with chains — zanjir-zani. Some draw blood from their own heads — tradition says this way began later, and Shia scholars themselves differ over it — some call it lawful, some forbid it. This book describes the ways of mourning as they are observed — it neither praises them nor condemns them.

Sunni Muslims also observe Ashura — but in a different way. Tradition says that on the day of Ashura Moses was saved from Pharaoh — so Sunnis fast on this day — it is recorded in the books of Hadith. The memory of Karbala is in the Sunni tradition too — but there it is observed not as mourning, rather as the memory of a martyrdom.

Ashura — two memories, one day

The tradition of fasting on Ashura — in memory of Moses' deliverance — is in a Hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim. The memory of Karbala — Husayn's martyrdom — is the second memory of the same day, joined to the date in al-Tabari's History. Both memories fall on the same day — and each is observed in its own tradition.

The ways of mourning — as they are observed

The description of sina-zani, zanjir-zani and drawing blood — as they are observed — is taken from the studies of modern scholars, like Heinz Halm's book on Shia Islam. The difference among Shia scholars over drawing blood is from the same study. This book gives no opinion on these ways.

Pause and think — Fourteen hundred years have passed since Karbala — and millions of people still weep for it today. Can a memory be so strong that it stays alive for centuries — and why?

8 · The Split Hardens — The Imamate and the Caliphate · · THE SPLIT HARDENS — THE IMAMATE AND THE CALIPHATE

After Karbala, two answers in the community became firm — two answers to the same question. The question was the same as on the day the Prophet died — who now? And now it had two answers — the Caliphate and the Imamate.

The Caliphate — the Sunni answer — says that after the Prophet the leader of the community is chosen by the people's choice — by a council, or by allegiance. The Caliph is a human being — he can be good, and he can also make mistakes. He is the guardian of the faith, but he is not infallible. And his task is — to apply the faith, and to keep the community one.

The Imamate — the Shia answer — says that after the Prophet the leader of the community is chosen by God — from the Prophet's house, the Ahl al-Bayt. The Imam is infallible — free of error — and he is the true explainer of the faith. The Imam is not only a ruler — he also gives the spiritual guidance of the faith.

This difference was not only of politics — it was a difference in how the faith is understood. Sunnis say — the faith is in the Quran and the Hadith, and to understand it there are scholars. Shias say — the faith is in the Quran and the Hadith, but to understand it rightly an Imam is needed — because only the Imam is the true heir of the faith.

Karbala filled this difference with pain. In Shia tradition Karbala is a martyrdom — a sacrifice that kept the faith alive. In Sunni tradition Karbala too is a martyrdom — but there it is a tragedy, an event that divided the community. Both remember Karbala — but in different ways.

The Imamate and the Caliphate — each in its own definition

The definition of the caliphate — a leader chosen by the people's choice — is Sunni tradition's. The definition of the Imamate — a leader chosen by God, infallible — is Shia tradition's. Both definitions are taken from the books of their own scholars — and this book records both in their own places, fully and honestly.

Who was right — this book's decision: no decision

This book does not decide whether the caliphate was right or the Imamate — whether Husayn should have pledged allegiance or not — whether Yazid's caliphate was lawful or not. These questions have been asked for fourteen hundred years — and to this day no single answer has been found. This book has recorded both answers in their own notes — and left the question open.

Pause and think — One question — who now? — and two answers. Does two answers mean one of them is wrong — or can there be something true in both?

9 · The Shia Branches — Twelve, Five, and Seven · · THE SHIA BRANCHES — TWELVERS, ZAYDIS, AND ISMAILIS

The Shia too are not one — with time, branches formed within the Shia tradition as well. Every branch's question was the same — which Imam? — and every branch's answer was different.

The Ithna Ashariya (Twelvers) — the largest branch — say there are twelve Imams — beginning with Ali and ending with Muhammad al-Mahdi, the twelfth Imam. Tradition says the twelfth Imam went into hiding in 874 — the Occultation — and that he will return one day. Until then his deputies — the scholars — guide the community. Today, most Shias in Iran, Iraq, Lebanon and Bahrain are Twelvers.

The Zaydiya (Fivers) — say there are five Imams — Ali, Hasan, Husayn, Ali Zayn al-Abidin, and then Zayd ibn Ali — who rose up against the Umayyads in 740 and was killed. Zaydis say the Imam is the one who rises up — who takes up the sword against wrong — not one who only sits and waits. Today, most Shias in Yemen are Zaydis.

The Ismailiya (Seveners) — say that after the sixth Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq, the Imam is his son Ismail — not his other son Musa. The Ismailis have their own long history — the Fatimid caliphate in Egypt, and then the Nizari and Musta'li branches. Today the Imam of the Nizari Ismailis is the Aga Khan — and the Musta'li Ismailis — the Bohras — are in India too.

The Twelvers — the count of twelve Imams

The list of the twelve Imams — Ali, Hasan, Husayn, Ali Zayn al-Abidin, Muhammad al-Baqir, Ja'far al-Sadiq, Musa al-Kazim, Ali al-Rida, Muhammad al-Jawad, Ali al-Hadi, Hasan al-Askari, and Muhammad al-Mahdi — is Shia tradition's, as recorded in al-Kulayni's al-Kafi and later Shia books. The year of the twelfth Imam's Occultation, 874 — is tradition's date.

The Zaydis — the count of five Imams

The Zaydi branch — five Imams, and Zayd ibn Ali's rising up in 740 — is Zaydi tradition's, as recorded in Heinz Halm's book on Shia Islam and Maria Dakake's study. That Zaydis say the Imam must rise up against wrong — that is the Zaydi tradition's own principle.

The Ismailis — the count of seven Imams

The Ismaili branch — holding Ismail to be the Imam after Ja'far al-Sadiq, the Fatimid caliphate, and the Nizari and Musta'li branches — is Ismaili tradition's, as recorded in the studies of Heinz Halm and Marshall Hodgson. That the Aga Khan is the Imam of the Nizari Ismailis — that is a fact of today.

Pause and think — One house — the house of Ali — and three different answers to which Imam. Can one question have three answers — and all three be true in their own place?

10 · The Sunni Schools — Four Paths, One Destination · · THE SUNNI SCHOOLS — FOUR PATHS, ONE DESTINATION

In the Sunni tradition too there is not one road only — four schools (madhhabs) of law were formed — and every school has its own teachers, its own books, and its own method.

Hanafi — named for Abu Hanifa (d. 767) — formed in Kufa. The Hanafi method is — along with the Quran and the Hadith, to use ra'y (reasoned opinion) and qiyas (analogy). Today, most Sunnis in Turkey, Central Asia, India and Pakistan are Hanafi.

Maliki — named for Malik ibn Anas (d. 795) — formed in Medina. The Maliki method is — the practice of the people of Medina — what was done in Medina is the best evidence of the faith. Today, most Sunnis in North and West Africa are Maliki.

Shafi'i — named for Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafi'i (d. 820) — formed in Egypt. The Shafi'i method is — to put the Quran and the Hadith highest, and to use qiyas in a firm method. Today, most Sunnis in Egypt, East Africa and South-East Asia are Shafi'i.

Hanbali — named for Ahmad ibn Hanbal (d. 855) — formed in Baghdad. The Hanbali method is — to put the Hadith highest, and to stay away from ra'y. Today, most Sunnis in Saudi Arabia are Hanbali.

All four schools hold each other to be right — none calls the other wrong. On one question the four may give different opinions — but all four are Sunni, all four read the same Quran, and all four follow the same Prophet.

The founders of the four schools — tradition's dates

The dates of death of the four founders — Abu Hanifa 767, Malik 795, al-Shafi'i 820, Ahmad ibn Hanbal 855 — are tradition's dates, from al-Tabari's History and later books of biography. Each school's method — ra'y, the practice of Medina, qiyas, Hadith — is taken from the studies of Marshall Hodgson and Fred Donner.

Pause and think — One Quran, one Prophet — and four different roads. Is having four roads to understand the faith a weakness — or a strength?

11 · What Both Hold in Common — The Quran, the Prophet, and the Five Pillars · · WHAT BOTH HOLD IN COMMON — THE QURAN, THE PROPHET, AND THE FIVE PILLARS

After so much difference, Sunni and Shia still have very much in common — so much that to an outsider, the two would look the same.

One Quran. Sunni and Shia read the same Quran — the same text, the same verses. On the text of the Quran there is no difference between the two.

One Prophet. Both hold Muhammad to be the last Prophet — and both hold his Sunna to be part of the faith.

The Five Pillars. Both say the Shahada (God is one, Muhammad is His messenger), both pray salah, both give zakat, both keep the fast, and both do the Hajj. All five pillars belong to both — and are the same for both.

Shias add one more line to the Shahada — 'Ali is the friend of God' — but it is not part of the Shahada, it is a separate testimony. And Shias fold their hands differently in prayer — and some Shias also give khums (the fifth part) in place of zakat. These are differences — but they do not break the Five Pillars.

And both remember Karbala — both hold Husayn to be a martyr — and both weep in his name. Karbala had divided the community — but Karbala is also the place where the two meet again.

The shared Quran — what the evidence says

That Sunni and Shia read the same Quran is a fact of evidence — the manuscripts of both traditions rest on the same text. There is no disagreement among scholars on this — both Marshall Hodgson and Heinz Halm record it.

The extra line in the Shia Shahada — Shia tradition's account

The adding of 'Ali is the friend of God' to the Shia Shahada is Shia tradition's — it is not part of the Shahada, it is a separate testimony. This is recorded in Heinz Halm's book on Shia Islam.

Pause and think — Both read the same Quran, follow the same Prophet, keep the same Five Pillars — and yet they are different. Are the things shared greater than the differences — or are the differences greater than the things shared?

Closing Reflection · · CLOSING REFLECTION

In this book we have seen — Muawiya, who made the caliphate into a kingdom; Hasan, who gave up the caliphate to stop a war; Yazid, who demanded allegiance; and Husayn, who did not pledge allegiance — and was killed at Karbala.

And we have seen that after Karbala the community walked two roads — Sunni and Shia — and on each road too branches formed — twelve, five, seven — and four schools.

In the next book we will see what happened after the Umayyads — the age of the Abbasids, and the golden age of Islam — when Baghdad was the greatest city in the world, and books were being written. But first, take one question with you —

In the field of Karbala, Husayn did not pledge allegiance — and was killed. Hasan made peace — and lived. Which road was right — the road of peace, or the road of martyrdom? There is no answer to this question in this book — and perhaps in no book at all.

Pause and think — What touched you most in this book — Hasan's peace, Husayn's journey, the silence of Karbala, Zaynab's speech, or the things both roads share? And why?

Sources · · SOURCES

The Quran — Surah Al Imran (3:144), Surah al-Ma'ida (5:3), Surah Yusuf (12:40).

Sahih al-Bukhari — the book of Hadith; the Hadith of the Ashura fast and the stories of early Islam are taken from it.

Sahih Muslim — the book of Hadith; the Hadith of the Ashura fast is taken from it too.

The Sunan of al-Tirmidhi (Jami) — the book of Hadith; the Hadith of Ghadir Khumm is recorded in it.

Al-Tabari's History (Ta'rikh al-Rusul wa'l-Muluk) — the greatest source of this book; Muawiya, the peace of Hasan, Yazid, Husayn's journey and the maqtal accounts of Karbala are taken from it.

Al-Baladhuri's Ansab al-Ashraf — on the people of early Islam and their stories; the stories of Hasan's peace and Muawiya are taken from it too.

Al-Kulayni's al-Kafi — the Shia book of Hadith; the list of the twelve Imams and Shia tradition are taken from it.

The maqtal accounts of Abu Mikhnaf (through al-Tabari) — the oldest source of the story of Karbala.

Wilferd Madelung, The Succession to Muhammad — on the question of succession, the peace of Hasan and Hasan's death.

Lesley Hazleton, After the Prophet — on the Saqifa, Ali, and the story of the first Fitna.

Fred Donner, Muhammad and the Believers — on early Islam and the kingdom of Muawiya's age.

Marshall Hodgson, The Venture of Islam (Volume 1) — on early Islam, the caliphate and the Sunni schools.

Maria Dakake, The Charismatic Community — on Shia tradition and the doctrine of the Imamate.

Heinz Halm, Shi'a Islam — on the Shia branches, the ways of mourning and Shia tradition.

Wherever this book says 'tradition says', the matter is taken from the books of the Seerah and the Hadith — not from the evidence of history. Where a matter rests on evidence, its name is given in a separate note. Where there are two opinions, both are recorded in their own notes — and the book has made no decision.
